utterances.text: Did there come a time later that day when the men from the town or village of Divic were assembled in front of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon whose instruction were they ordered to assemble there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The army, the unit that came into the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many men were assembled in front of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Approximately 100 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you among that group of 100?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in front of the mosque at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They asked for weapons to be handed over. I don't know how many weapons they were actually looking for. And if we could not give the weapons to them, then they -- then people were supposed to hand these weapons over secretly, if I can put it that way, at a particular place they said near the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were weapons handed over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they conduct a search of houses for additional weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, while we were in front of the mosque, other soldiers were searching houses, looking for things in houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to now draw your attention to the next day. Could you please describe what occurred on that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The next day the army was replaced by the police and - how should I put this? - they were on duty there after the military. They imposed a curfew. It was from 10.00 or 11.00 in the evening until 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning. Then we could go to the town of Zvornik with our personal IDs, and then in town we got past passes which made it possible for us to move about town. After awhile, we managed to get passes that were valid in the Republic of Serbia, namely in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was issuing these passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: These passes were first issued at the Drina Hotel in Zvornik, and after that, at the SUP in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they were issued at the Drina Hotel, who was the person or what function did that person serve who issued these passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The person wore civilian clothes, and I don't know what position this person held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the pass -- were you yourself issued with a pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pass that you were issued with, would it have allowed you to have travelled outside the municipality of either Zvornik or Mali Zvornik? Could you have gone further than those two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, and I didn't try to go further either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serbian police that you describe, were they members of the local police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the police no longer appeared to be in charge but they appeared to have been replaced by the army once again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you give us some idea about when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Around the 22nd of May. The police was replaced by the military. I don't know the military people who came in, but they started creating problems in Divic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you to speak a little more loudly. Could I ask you to describe in a little more detail what you mean when you refer to the creation of problems.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, for example, they stopped women in the street and they took away their jewellery. They drove away the cars we had. They went to people's houses looking for money. They searched houses. They took away everything they could take away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, from the period of time when the men were gathered in front of the mosque and surrendered weapons until this time now in -- towards the end of May, was there any armed resistance from the people of Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time during this period when a number of buses came into the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: When this military came in after the police, they said to us that we were not safe in that place and that they should move us out. They told us that we had two hours. In the meantime, buses arrived, about 11 of them, and they said that they would transfer us to Olovo, to the town of Olovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is Olovo located with respect to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: On the road to Sarajevo. It's closer to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how many people from Divic were placed on these buses to be taken to Olovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: About 500 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that include people of all -- of both sexes and of all ages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes; men, women, children of all ages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these 500, were they all Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the bus able to reach Olovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the bus have to turn around and return to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: At Han Pijesak, we were stopped. We waited for about two hours, and we were told that we simply could not go on, that there was some kind of fighting going on there or whatever. Then they returned us to Zvornik, and we were stopped yet again between Milici and Vlasenica where we spent the night. The second day, we arrived in Zvornik and we waited for about an hour or two in front of the SUP building. Then they took us in the direction of Tuzla. We came to an elevation or, rather, a place we called Crni Vrh. That is where we were stopped yet again. We waited for about an hour and then we were returned to Zvornik, to the Zvornik bus station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time or when did you return to Zvornik after the second attempt to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Around midday, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened upon your return to Zvornik for the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Upon our arrival in front of the bus station, the military men who were there ordered us to get off the bus, all the men, that is, then they separated us, that is to say those who were older than 60 and younger than 18, the way they saw it. Then they returned others to the bus, and those who were not taken by bus were taken to the sports stadium in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men that were separated from the rest of the group, can you tell us approximately how many men were in that group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: One hundred seventy-four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you taken to a building, a specific building near the sports stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Not far away from the stadium. Right by the Zvornik municipality. This is the administration building of a company called Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were all of the group of 174 men placed into that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. We were put into a room that was too small to take so many people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were addressed by the Serb mayor of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Brano Grujic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he say to yourself and the other men in that room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He said that the names of the people who were there should be recorded, that we would get something to do, that we would go out to do something, and that we should sign some kind of paper recognising the government that came in or, rather, some kind of loyalty certificate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign such a certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did other men in the building or in the room sign that certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think that no one signed it. They didn't even ask for it later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when 11 men were removed from that room and you never saw those 11 men again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. After awhile, after we had stayed there for about a few hours, two soldiers came who explained they were looking for ten homeowners who were supposed to accompany them on the search of their houses, and then another ten, and that this would go on until they had checked all the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken from that room to search your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that room before you were taken from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: We spent two nights there, and we were there for about two and a half days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described the room as being too small for the number of people in it. Can I ask you in a sentence or two to give the Chamber some idea about the conditions inside that room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: There was enough room for all of us to stand up. All of us could not sit or lie down or any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you fed while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you characterise the amount of food that you were given?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Very, very little. I think there was some kind of spread to put on bread, and I think that there was marmalade jam, whatever, there was something sweet. Afterwards, a soldier said to us that we would get a bit more food, after awhile that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken from this room, where were you brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They told us to get out of that room and to board the buses that were in front over there in Zvornik, and then they transferred us to Celopek or, rather, the cultural centre at Celopek. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Celopek is the name of another village or another area in the Zvornik municipality; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the cultural centre, would you please describe the type -- what would be the ordinary purpose that a building called the cultural centre would be used for in this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The bus station was where the cultural centre was. It was the local bus station. There was also a store, and there was a restaurant. There was a building behind this store, and that's where the cultural centre was. There was a stage in the building, and behind this building was a small room that was used as a toilet. And next to that building was yet another restaurant, or a smallish room that was used as a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were used to move you and others up to the Celopek Dom Kulture centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Two or three buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were -- were there guards, armed guards accompanying the men as they were transported to the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many men altogether, approximate if you need to, were transported from the room up to the Celopek Dom cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: One hundred sixty-two men were transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution will be tendering a binder of exhibits with four photographs. Could I ask that a number be assigned at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 438.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the witness be shown - we'll use the Sanction system, if it works today - that his monitor be set accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you take a look at the photograph before you. It's Prosecution Exhibit 438, tab 1. Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. That's the building where we were detained, the first one. You can see that it's a dilapidated building, the first one. It was used as a toilet. The other one is the cultural centre, and then there's the bus station and the restaurant and the store. The other one on the left-hand side is this smallish restaurant or, rather, this smallish room that was used as a restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that in front of the building furthest away from us in the photograph, that that is the road connecting Celopek and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: This road that you can see on the side is some kind of a small road, whereas the other one is the main road that goes through Celopek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the road I'm referring to, the main road. Is that the road that is visible at the back of the building, or the front of the building, as it were?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, that's the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying the photographer who took that picture was standing at the back of the building or the complex of buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to look at Prosecution Exhibit 438, tab 2. Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: What is depicted is the bus station, the building where the store was, the restaurant, and behind that building was this cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Prosecution Exhibit 438, tab 3. Is this one of the buildings that make up part of that complex where you were held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. That building was used as a toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in the Dom Kulture centre at Celopek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: About a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a person by the name of Dusan Repic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Before the war, I did not know this person, but during my stay in Batkovic, I found out that this person who came to the cultural centre in Celopek was called Dusan Repic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at Prosecution Exhibit 438, tab 4, on the screen in front of you. Do you recognise the person depicted in those photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. That's the person named Repic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to describe some of the events that occurred while you were kept in captivity in Celopek, and let me begin by asking you to describe generally the living conditions under which you and the other men were kept during your period of incarceration there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The conditions were more than bad. The first day we came we had some kind of thin mattresses. We did not have enough water. We did not have enough food. At the beginning we could go out to the toilet and we could sit in front of the building, but then they forbade that too. The first few days we didn't get food at all and then we asked the guards who were there -- we gave them money and we asked them to buy something for us to eat. They brought us very little food, and they never brought us any change. This room had about 10 windows that were closed, it had two doors. One door was always locked, and the other one that we used was locked with a chain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the times that these doors were not locked, were there armed guards at the facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The guards were in front of the building. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the building of the Dom Kulture centre was on a road, a busy road upon which traffic frequently travelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the people that were detained in Celopek were forced to give up all of their identification papers and any other personal documents that they may have had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. At first some of the soldiers, I don't know exactly which ones, asked for us to hand over our belts and shoelaces. Then a group came asking us for -- to hand over all our documents and everything we had; money, jewellery, all the documents we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men that asked you to hand over the documents and everything that you had, did you recognise them as being from the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I did not recognise them. I don't know where they came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to identify their accents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Their accents were Serbian, coming from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when fathers and sons were made to line up and to record their names, identifying them as father and son?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. That's what they were required to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who initiated this? Who -- who were the people that made these fathers and sons identify themselves as such?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The person called Repic, with his group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father detained with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your uncle detained with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this period, did members of Repic's group interrogate some of the men that were being detained in the centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: There was another group there that came several times. Sometimes they came together. I don't know whether it was exactly that group or Repic's group, but people were interrogated, and they were asking for weapons too. That's what they asked for more, for weapons, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of these interrogations, were some of the people being interrogated killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The people who were taken out, I don't know exactly. Shots could be heard. I don't know whether they were killed. They took out two men, we heard two shots. After that, they took out a man to see what was happening, and he told us that those men had been killed. Then he said that if we didn't surrender our weapons, the same fate would befall us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This other group that you referred to, did you learn where they came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: We later learnt that these men came from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Loznica is located in what country, what republic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: In the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when men in the building were subjected to brutal treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd asked you to please describe --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Not once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to please describe what types of treatment you observed while you were detained in that room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I saw them asking for fathers and sons to get on the stage, to take off their clothes, to strip, and to engage in oral sex using their mouths and genitals. At first it had to be fathers with sons, and after that, sons with fathers. The people who applied, some were fathers and sons, others were not. At first it appeared that the group was too small. Then they asked or, rather, separated people at random, at will, sending them to the stage and to join the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many pairs of fathers and sons were forced to engage in this type of activity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Two or three pairs of fathers and sons, but the total was about eight to ten couples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the other men in the building required to do while this was taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The other men were ordered to sit facing the stage, and they all had to watch what was going on on the stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened if one of the other men in the room did not look at what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They required that they watch and follow the happenings on the stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you approximate for us, as best you can recall, when this occurred, during what period of your detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: This was roughly between the 10th and the 11th of June. That was when we celebrate our religious holiday Bajram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when some of the men were forced to perform even more violent acts against each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They demanded that certain couples, certain men, bite off the genitals of others. They asked men to show those penises. They actually forced a man to show the penis he had bitten off and to swallow it. One man refused to, but the other one did actually do it. And then they asked one person to -- to push the broom -- the handle of a broom into the behind of another man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to these acts, were -- were men also mutilated with knives?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we get there, we should identify who it was who gave these orders. It's described as "they," but we should learn more detail who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would ask you to answer Judge May's question. When you used the word "they," could you please describe who specifically are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The group of the person known as Repic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Repic himself personally present when these acts that you've described occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, he was present, and he took out those men and he demanded that sons and fathers come out. He selected them. And all those happenings, he was the one who gave the orders for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when members of this group used knives to mark the bodies of some of the men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please describe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: On the stage, I don't think it was on that day, but on that day, they killed men who were there. After that, the men on the stage had their -- the meat between their fingers cut. They would stab the men's thighs, and they would stab people's hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You yourself, were you subjected to any of this treatment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. They stabbed through one hand. The other one, the knife didn't go right through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know the identity of the person who -- or the name of the person who stabbed you in your hands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know his proper name but he was a large man, rather heavy but not tall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Repic's group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because they never all came together. Sometimes there would be two groups together, sometimes three, sometimes only one, but they were not always the same group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the treatment that you've described for us, were there also times when random shots were fired into the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, when they demanded that sons and fathers come out to do what they did, Repic was armed with a small calibre rifle, and he shot at people, who did not survive, that is, the people Repic hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your entire stay at Celopek, on approximately how many occasions did this type of treatment of the people detained there occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: You mean killings or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sexual abuse and the killings. On approximately how many different occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The sexual abuse happened on that one day, and the killings happened on two days or, rather, several men were killed on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were members of the group also made to have fistfights with each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father one of the people that was ordered to -- to have a fistfight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. He was also ordered to come out, and he had his pair who was his next door neighbour, and before they were ordered to do this, they said that they would beat them if they refused to fight one another. And as they simply couldn't hit each other, then they beat them. So then this neighbour was in a coma for two days. After that, he passed away, whereas my father was badly beaten up. He was black and blue all over from these blows he had received, and he can't even remember everything that happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ultimately happened to your uncle who you said was detained in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That first occasion, my two uncles did not survive. On Bajram, that is the night between the 10th and the 11th, the two uncles did not survive. One was dead and the other one -- his heart was still beating, but he passed away. He was hit in the forehead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what ultimately happened to your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He was killed too or, rather, he died in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances surrounding his death.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: On that day when my father lost his life -- this happened around the 26th of June. I think it was the Serbian holiday, St. Vitus Day. I don't know exactly. It happened in the afternoon, around 1600 hours. We received the food, our rations, which we didn't manage to eat when Repic arrived with an automatic rifle in his hand. He, as usual, demanded that we talk about people he was looking for from Kula Grad to Zvornik. He fired a burst not far from me. Three men fell from the shots. Two got up wounded, not seriously. And this one who couldn't get up, he remained on the ground. He came up to him and shot him with a pistol. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. After that, he went on demanding that we talk about these people, and then he opened fire at random at the people, and he started killing them. Then there was one burst of fire, then another one. And on that occasion, he killed some 20 men and wounded about 22 others. After that, when he ordered that everything be cleaned up, I found my father lying there, and I saw that he was no longer alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of your detention at Celopek, did a Serb friend of yours come to the centre and have a brief conversation with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. He was my school fellow. His name was Goran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to summarise what it was he said to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He called me out and he asked me whether we needed anything, and I told him we needed water because we were short of it as we would get about two canisters of water a day. Then I asked him to protect at least my father, if he couldn't protect me, as I was younger. And then he told me that he thought that what had happened would not be repeated and that the SUP of Zvornik had intervened and that the key would be handed in to the SUP of Zvornik and that from then on people would not be able to enter the building as they had been doing up until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were taken from Celopek and brought somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. That second time when some 20 men were killed, maybe the following day or two days later the rest of the men who were there, together with those who were wounded, were transferred to the old prison in Zvornik, and we spent about 15 days there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did there come a time when you were transferred from that prison to another location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: After spending time in the old prison in Zvornik, we were transferred to Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that another prison camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. It was a larger camp than the one in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately when were you transferred to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Around about the middle of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long were you detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: About a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe for the Chamber the conditions at Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: It was a building, quite a large building, which was used to store seeds for agricultural purposes. The windows were closed, and they were closed up with steel blinds. We slept on straw covered with a blanket, and we had nothing to cover ourselves with. The compound had a wire fence. We had a couple of water taps and one open toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people that were detained there, can you provide us with some details about that, the approximate people that you were aware were detained there as well as the range of ages and whether both men and women were detained at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The age of the people, most of them were able-bodied. There were two women at first - I think one was there with her husband - and then they were taken somewhere. I don't know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you present when members of the Red Cross, International Committee of the Red Cross visited Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what, if anything, occurred prior to visits by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Before they arrived, their arrival would be announced. It was announced a couple of times but they didn't come. But each time, before they were due to arrive, old people over 60 and youngsters under 18 were hidden, and a group that they called "special cases" were also taken away somewhere. Where, I don't know exactly, but they weren't present when the Red Cross came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would they be returned after the Red Cross left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, they would be returned to the compound when the Red Cross left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask at this time that a copy of Prosecution Exhibit 336, pages 28 and 29, be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to take the pointer at your right hand. Do you recognise what is depicted on this map, this copy of Prosecution Exhibit 336?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: It is a map of a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is not complete. And I recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I ask the director to zoom in on the right hand portion on that page. You will see some red circles.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Handwriting" not "signature."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the circles on the page, did you make those red circles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, I did?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask the director just to zoom out a little bit so we can see all of the circles. And that is good. Maybe we can adjust the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these the locations that you have testified about here today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask you to start at the top and please just point to the different locations and just call out the name of each individual location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: This place here is the place where I was born, Divic. This place here is the place where I was detained for a month and where the killings and sexual abuse took place. After that, we were taken to Batkovic, which is here, not far from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could I ask you -- you haven't circled it, but could you just point to where the town of Zvornik is located.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've referred to Mali Zvornik. Could you please indicate that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to return to Celopek for a minute. Could I ask you to summarise for us how many men were killed that you saw? Could you summarise for us with an approximate number how many men were killed at Celopek during your detention there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Approximately some 30 men. All those killings took place in the room in which we were detained. As for the people that were taken out, I don't know whether they were killed. I saw some of them, three or four of them. As for the others, I never saw them again nor have I heard of them since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many men who were detained there are you aware of were subjected to sexual abuse of the type you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Some 30 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after your release from custody, did you come to learn some years later that Mr. Repic was the subject of a prosecution in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. I read that in a newspaper. I don't know exactly which one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the subject of that prosecution in part the crimes that you've described for us as having occurred in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, that was the subject of that prosecution, and I think that I read that he confessed that he had killed eight men. How the trial ended, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that prosecution was conducted in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere near Sabac, I think. In that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the outcome of that case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, is it a Defence Exhibit 56 which deals with this? If you could check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just have a look at the number of this witness, because the witness was not protected to begin with up until today. 1164; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1461. Right. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1461, let's clear something up first, this key issue with respect to the crimes that took place and that you described as having taken place in Celopek. Do you know the name of the man whose nickname was Repic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: "Pigtail" in translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I learnt about that name while I was detained in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Dusan Vuckovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dusan Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic, right. That agrees with the information I have. Do you know that this particular man was at the head of a group of criminals, criminals who perpetrated a number of crimes in the area that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that it was precisely the authorities in Serbia who got news of their criminal behaviour, this kind of criminal behaviour that they engaged in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: All I know was that legal proceedings were brought against that individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That is the consequence of the fact that I've just mentioned. Do you know that this man Vuckovic, nicknamed Repic or pigtail, and as we saw his photograph, I assume he was called Repic because he wore this pigtail, that he was a citizen of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt about that in Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It doesn't matter where you learnt of it. I'm just asking whether you know about it. And do you know that it was on the basis of the facts that they were citizens of Serbia, in fact, for which the authorities in Serbia learnt they had committed some crimes on the territory of Bosnia, that these people were in fact arrested? They were taken into custody by the authorities of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know that these people were taken to trial at the District Court in Sabac for war crimes, in fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I read about this for Repic in the papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You read it in the papers. Right. Now, do you know that they were tried as far as back as 1993 on the basis of the facts that, following the Criminal Code of our country, war crimes are the gravest crimes, considered to be the gravest crimes and that according to the information that the authorities had, this man and his collaborators had perpetrated those crimes, so he was arrested and he was tried precisely for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why he was arrested, but it said in the papers that yes, he was accused for having perpetrated the crimes in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you read about this in the papers, but we can find the documents. I don't want to enter into that now. But you presented some of the atrocities that you saw happen and experienced yourself. So I'm not going to ask you about that because I think Mr. Groome asked you about that at great length. I just want to ask you whether you are aware of the fact that when the authorities in Serbia learnt about these crimes, arrested those people and took them to trial and tried them for war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well -- Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we have documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Don't interrupt. We have the papers. We will have them recorded. It's thought they're D56. During the adjournment, it may be that we can actually track that down. So there's no point asking the witness about them. It's simply something he read, whereas we have the papers. Yes. Now, let's move on, if you want to, to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely because I know that the opposite side is well aware of the fact that these people were arrested by the authorities of Serbia and taken to trial and tried for war crimes, I don't then understand why this witness has been brought here to testify against me, because the authorities in Serbia prosecuted the war crimes that he has just described. But let's go back to the beginning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you any questions -- look, we'll hear your speeches in due course. We're not here for that now. Now, as you've said, this witness has come here and given very difficult evidence. So I suggest you deal with his cross-examination as expeditiously as you can. I take it there is no dispute about his evidence about what happened in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, as to what happened in Celopek, the authorities of Serbia, on the basis of the knowledge they had, arrested these people and the courts tried them. So I don't want to go back to that topic. What I want to do is to go back to the beginning of the testimony of Mr. B-1461 related to the issues he talked about and the circumstances he described with respect to the attacks on the village of Divic and all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1461, was there a political party that acted in an organised fashion in Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I'm not a politician. I don't really know whether there was a political party, but as far as I know, I don't think there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this may I take it that you were never a member of a party at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the organisation of the Patriotic League that had its representatives in Divic? Just give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. At the beginning, in response to a question from Mr. Groome, you said that in Zvornik a rally was held which was devoted to peace, life together, and some positive goals taken by and large, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the meeting held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Roughly around the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 7th of April? That means just one day after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, I don't know when it was recognised exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of April. And then the rally was held in Zvornik on the 7th of April for a life together with no ethnic conflicts and so on. Well, in your opinion, would you say that the population of Zvornik had opted to preserve Yugoslavia and a life of communality within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: At the rally, yes, we could see that people were in favour of life together and for peace, a life in common and conditions of peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean then that the people of Zvornik, both Muslims and Serbs alike who had lived there, were opposed to the SDA positions and Alija Izetbegovic who favoured the separation of Bosnia from Yugoslavia, its secession and everything else that happened and led up to the crisis that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what they were in favour of, but they were in favour of peace, and they said they didn't need any kind of war and that quite simply people wanted to live a peaceful life, like they did before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that. I believe that people strove to ensure that, because anybody normal would be in favour of peace. You say that the war in Zvornik - and you say this on page 2 of your statement, paragraph 5 - began on the 8th of April. So on the 6th of April Bosnia and Herzegovina was given recognition, on the 7th of April you held a rally in favour of a life together, and the conflict broke out on the 8th of April; is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, who created that conflict? Who caused the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I wasn't there, nor do I know who caused it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that it was at the multi-party elections that came before all these events the Serbs won the majority in Zvornik, the SDS party in fact, that they had the majority vote?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I know nothing about politics, and I was not a politician of any kind, and I think you would have to ask one of the politicians that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I'm asking you because you can't tell me who caused the crisis. Does it seem to you to be logical that the Serbs who had the authority in Zvornik, that it was up to them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to win over power and authority if they had already had it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given you his answer to this. He's not involved in it, it's pointless to ask him further questions, particularly of that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sort. And it may not assist us very much as to who started it. The real point of his evidence concerns partly Divic, of course, but also about what happened when he was in detention and the conditions which existed there. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, what happened during his detention I myself and the authorities in Serbia personally consider to be a war crime, and those crimes were tried in Serbia ten years ago. So I have nothing to ask him on that score as to the details, because to every normal man -- everybody normal would feel sick and feel sick listening to the details that were put forward. It's enough to turn one's stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: The fighting for Zvornik, as you say, went on for two days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you weren't there at the time. You were in Divic all the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your statement that the fighting took place between the Serb army and the Muslim inhabitants. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, then. These Muslim inhabitants, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know what they had, but I heard from people -- I heard about it from people who came from Zvornik to Divic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these Muslim forces, did they fight in an organised fashion? Who was their commander? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I have no information about that nor do I know whether it was organised or unorganised. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know whether in Zvornik a Muslim Crisis Staff had been set up perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, in Zvornik I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know about that. And do you know whether those Muslim forces had any form of heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that in the fighting in Zvornik there were no people who were wounded or killed, no casualties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: According to what the people who had come from there said, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no casualties; no persons killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think in my statement I say that I don't know actually whether there were any persons killed or wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Rasim Juzbasic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a deputy in the BH Assembly and he was from Zvornik, that is to say from your parts, but you say you don't know him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who Izet Mehinagic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I worked in the field, I went round to do my job, so I don't really know the people from the municipality that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But do you know -- you read the papers, I assume, and listened to the radio. Do you know that these two people at a press conference held in Tuzla - and that took place on the 10th of April, 1992, and it was published by the Sarajevo daily Oslobodjenje -- I assume you read the daily papers, Sarajevo Oslobodjenje - said that they had just come from Zvornik and that the Serb forces had a lot of casualties, wounded and killed, and that the Muslim forces, up until their departure, had about 15 persons injured and one person killed. That's what they said, according to the writings of the Oslobodjenje paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that does not coincide with what you learnt about and what you testified about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then tell me this: If there were armed conflicts indeed and if they went on for two days, does that mean that there were two sides shooting at each other, at one another?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what the conflicts were, whether they were clashes between two parties, two sides, or what. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. 1461. You say that the conflicts between the Serb army and the Muslim citizens in Zvornik, that's how you refer to them. Now, this Serbian army, can we call it the citizens of Zvornik of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, we could put it that way too. I don't know who those people were actually, the people who came from Zvornik who informed us about that either, of the events in Zvornik. They didn't know who --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't know them or they didn't know? Well, in Zvornik, was it not a conflict between the Serbs and Muslims or, rather, wasn't this part of the civil war that had started after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the beginning of the attack on the army throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Wasn't that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know why the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Can you testify at all about anything linked to these conflicts in Zvornik, because as you yourself say now and in your statement that when all this was going on, all this fighting was going on, you never actually left Divic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, I was there until I left, until they moved us out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw nothing that actually went on in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So everything you're telling us is on the basis of what you heard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who brought this information to you from Zvornik? Can you give us a name and surname of the person who told you about all this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they some locals who came to inform you, or did somebody else come from Zvornik to inform you about what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think they were people from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Groome whether you came to the conclusion that something was happening in Zvornik when you saw some corpses flowing down the Drina River. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He asked me whether I assumed that something was happening somewhere else when I saw corpses flowing down the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but he mentioned Zvornik specifically in his question, and you can check that on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going to adjourn, but before we do, Judge Kwon has the exhibit to which we referred earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It was Defence Exhibit 56 under seal, which seems to be a report of the district public prosecutor's office of Republic of Serbia in Sabac, and it is a request to the District Court investigating judge asking that an investigation is to be conducted against Mr. Vojin Vuckovic and Dusko Vuckovic, also known as Repic. But the report only deals with these killings, torturings, but it does not mention about the sexual abuse. I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me return that to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can later get some indictment or formal documents later, can we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is in possession of some of the documents, and whatever the Prosecution is in possession of we will produce to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps the legal officer would come up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A document was mentioned a short while ago that had to do with the criminal prosecution of the perpetrators of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. 1461, you said you only heard about this from the newspapers. Were you perhaps informed of the fact that the attitude towards paramilitary formations and such groups was generally the attitude of the authorities of the government, that is, of Yugoslavia, of Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I'm not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just going to read something out to you, part of the order of the then Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav army, Colonel General Zivota Panic. This is an order dated the 1st of August, 1992. This is roughly the time when this news could have reached the Yugoslav authorities because it coincides with the time you have been referring to. I am reading this out to you to ask you whether you knew anything about that or whether you learned anything about it later, because I see that in the meantime, you had been in a camp. Inter alia, I'm going to skip all the explanations that come before hand and I'm now just going to read the following: "I hereby order to the 2nd Army, and also could the 1st and 3rd Armies please be notified in cooperation with the Ministries of the Interior of Serbia and Montenegro, immediately establish an operative staff for following the situation on the ground and for taking all measures to stop the activity of individuals, groups, and all other paramilitary formations." I'm asking the interpreters whether this should be read out again. The English booth said it's not necessary for now. All right. Very well. I continue reading: "According to one's assessments, these staffs should be set up in towns and garrisons that are in the directions facing the border crossings towards Bosnia-Herzegovina and, if necessary, within one's area of responsibility. The units should be made capable of rapid deployment and action for controlling territory on all important intersections and directions that are carried out from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Joint checkpoints should be established and also mobile patrols should be established and should be given concrete assignments. All mobile units of the army of Yugoslavia and of the Ministries of the Interior -" it is Serbia and Montenegro that are being referred to - "should be announced in a timely fashion. Unannounced groups should be stopped, asked to show their IDs, and disarmed. One should bear in mind that these paramilitary units all use the army uniform of Yugoslavia, and they are prone to violent behaviour and crime, which makes it necessary to be cautious and to act efficiently, including the use of firearms." So that is the order of the Chief of General Staff that has to do with this. So it's not only something that had to do with the prosecutor's office, the authorities, the civilian authorities, but also the military structures, that is to say from the top, from the General Staff further down. Also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you're here asking questions. What is the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information about that too --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would like to read part of the order of the commander of the 1st Army, and that is relevant to the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I can't see the point if you're reading out something to a witness who has never heard of the order. He's not a member of your army or anything else. So how he's supposed to answer to it, I don't know. You can call evidence about this in due course, but there's no point putting it to witnesses who know nothing about it at all. So move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I think the document has been exhibited already. If the Prosecution could tell us the number. The order disbanding the paramilitary formations by Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We're looking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to point out, Mr. May, that in these orders reference is made to the fact that these groups and units should be stopped, asked to show their IDs, and disarmed. So that is the order. And it should also be borne in mind that paramilitary formations most often use the uniforms of the army of Yugoslavia and that they include persons who are prone to violent and criminal behaviour and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. This isn't a general debate. This is a witness who is giving evidence about specific events. Now, you can call your evidence -- it may be, as Judge Kwon has pointed out, that this document is already in evidence, so there's no need to go over it again. Now, have you got any questions specific to this witness, or otherwise we should let him go rather than detain him here longer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. There are questions for this witness that have to do with the rest of his testimony, but, Mr. May, since these documents were not tendered, would you accept having them tendered now into evidence, because they have to do the same thing from the military point of view and from the police point of view. That is to say the activities of the military and police of Serbia and Montenegro in view of the activities of the paramilitary formations referred to here. And also the way in which these paramilitary formations are being treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: At the moment, there is no connection with this witness, and they can't be introduced through him. You can introduce them through a witness who knows something about them. But there's no point with this witness. Also, we'll check to see if these documents haven't already been introduced. Now, let's move on. Let's move on to another topic. We can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. return to the documents in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, these documents have to do with the phenomenon about which this witness is testifying, not the witness himself. This has to do with general documents that deal with the phenomenon that the witness is testifying about. So I believe that this is quite a legitimate request to have these documents introduced into evidence. And of course you can refuse to do that. That is up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see from your statements that the Muslims from Divic established a Crisis Staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. When they felt that something was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, how many members did this Crisis Staff have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Approximately three or four members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they from the Party of Democratic Action or from the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know if they were in any party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know anything about the criteria according to which Crisis Staff members were chosen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. As far as I can see from your statement, your Crisis Staff was linked to the Crisis Staffs of other villages and towns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: According to their statements, I think that once or twice they spoke to the Crisis Staff at Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way did they contact these other staffs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Crisis Staff, did it have anything to do with the collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what you say on page 2, paragraph 6, you got some weapons from Zvornik, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: According to their statements, something came either from the local commune or the municipality of Zvornik, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know which persons actually brought these weapons to you from Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where these weapons came from? Do you know where they originated from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such weapons were distributed in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how weapons from Zvornik were brought to Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know about that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know whether weapons were sent to you from Zvornik at their initiative or was it your Crisis Staff that had asked for weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your Crisis Staff, who was in charge of distributing weapons in Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get any weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that your Crisis Staff organised patrols; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many such patrols were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Approximately perhaps three or four patrols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people made up a single patrol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think two respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of organising these patrols and these military activities? You mentioned the name of Rasim Zahirovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in charge of these patrols and military activities in Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He was the one who communicated with the people and this Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And who was it from the Crisis Staff or in the organisation of the Crisis Staff that trained these members of these groups that carried weapons? Who trained them to use weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think that there was no training. And who did the training is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever on any one of these patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I was at home all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At home all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And do you know whether during these patrols some of these people who were on the patrols were in a position to engage in fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see from your statement that in your village there were only eight Serbs who lived there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From a total population of 2.500?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you because Mr. Groome had asked you whether these people who then left were Muslims. So practically your village was a purely Muslim village almost. So they only could have been Muslims. And what was the attitude towards these eight Serbs? Was anybody in charge of watching them or checking on them in any way at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't think that they had any problems because these are people from mixed marriages who lived together with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In your statement you say that as soon as the fighting stopped in Zvornik, the locals in Divic started fleeing from the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many locals from the village of Divic left it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think that everybody left it, practically everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But on page 2, in the last paragraph, you say that after you had evacuated your family you returned to Divic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did that because, as you say, you wanted to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Not to see what was going on. I actually wanted to see what was going on with the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there some kind of obligation on your part for you to return in view of the positions of this Crisis Staff of Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you returned of your own free will. Did anybody else return in addition to you? Because you say that all the locals had left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think that everybody got out. Perhaps a few people stayed behind, and afterwards, almost everybody returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true that those who returned saw that nothing had happened in Divic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to Mr. Groome's question, the one that I've already raised, and then we were interrupted. Something was going on in Zvornik, and you saw that there were corpses in the Drina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I did see corpses in the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this couldn't have had anything to do with Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think that these corpses could not travel upstream, they could only move downstream.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you, because Divic is upstream from Zvornik, so it couldn't have had anything to do with Zvornik. So how many corpses did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but we reported a few of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: About 20 or 30. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the basis of what did you conclude that these were Muslims who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I did not say that they were Muslims, but I did say that these were dead persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they could have been either Serbs or Muslims or both.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3, in paragraph 3 of your statement you say that a certain Ahmet - I think it's Srndic - went to Amajic, a Serb village, to see an acquaintance of his.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was supposed to guarantee Srndic's security so that the man could go to Serbia to buy cigarettes. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's what he agreed upon with this man from Amajic, that he would help him buy cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Could you clarify something for me in this respect: This was happening at a time when, as far as I understood your statement, expected an attack to take place against your village and when you said that they were attacking Kula Grad, this fortification, that the village was under siege, that the villagers were leaving it for fear of their own lives, and this man Ahmed Srndic, through a Serb village, goes to Serbia to buy cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
