utterances.text: Since we were out off from town and we did not have any resources, I don't know how they got in touch, but I imagine that they knew each other from before and this Ahmet worked in Amajic, and I think they simply agreed that they help each other out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this must be the most passionate smoker I'd ever heard of. Under all these circumstances, he reaches agreements to go to Serbia to buy cigarettes. His village is under siege and there was shooting, and he goes to Serbia to buy cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: At that time there wasn't any shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Srndic was arrested on the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how was he arrested when he returned to the village the very same afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, but he was escorted from the Zvornik hydroelectric power station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he returned to the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They returned him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that a certain Major Marko Pavlovic came with him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the name of that man or was his name different? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything about that, but the Crisis Staff people said how he had introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so how he introduced himself. Introduced himself as Marko Pavlovic and as a major?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, Major Marko Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you infer on the basis of that that he was a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He was wearing military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that he came to persuade the members of the Crisis Staff to have the armed people from your village hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain to you why the surrender of weapons was required at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He didn't give me any explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, did anybody attack the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody shoot at the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Men from the other side of the Drina River, from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. According to my information, it is from this location that is called Kula Grad, which was a kind of fortified place where there was a unit of Muslim forces, fire was opened from there on positions of the army of Yugoslavia on the other bank of the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you not aware of it or do you believe that it is not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know whether fire was opened from Kula Grad on Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And how many people were killed in the village during that attack that you described? Was anyone killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think no one was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So no one was killed. You say that two days after their first arrival, this man who introduced himself as Major Pavlovic, he again organised a meeting to discuss the same issue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you get information from about those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: From people in the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he threaten or intimidate the people there? What was the substance of that talk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know about any threats, but the content was that he repeated the demand for weapons to be handed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know to what extent that Crisis Staff and the unit in Kula Grad was armed, how many men they had under arms, under their control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as I can see, they advised you not to hand in your weapons. And then you say, "While Kula Grad was in Muslim hands, Divic has nothing to fear." That would be roughly what you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That was their opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have no idea or information as to how many of them were there nor that they opened fire across the Drina River on positions held by the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, I have no information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you then come to the conclusion, without having any information, on what basis they were guaranteeing your security if you don't know how many of them there were nor who they are nor what kind of weapons they have? Because that would mean that should Divic be attacked, they would be the ones to defend you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me not ask you any more questions about that then since you say you don't know. And those attempts to remove weapons were actually attempts to resolve the problems that had cropped up in the area by peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of attempts those were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the representatives of the Serb forces, that morning when Divic was attacked, did they propose that you surrender your weapons? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. They demanded that over the loudspeaker, speaking from the Serbian side of the river, that we surrender our weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it clear to you then that this was because there was shooting on the other side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know why they made that demand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how then would they know that you were armed if you weren't firing at them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see anything connected to the opening of fire on positions held by the army of Yugoslavia from your side? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: From our side, I did not see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But all in all, no one was killed in that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4, in paragraph 4, you say that members of the Crisis Staff fled from the village and took the weapons away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything stay behind which the locals handed in later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think there was some private weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Only private ones. And do you know the answer to the question why members of the Crisis Staff had left? Why didn't they stay in Divic like the other inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know why they left, but I do know why they came back, because they were there when the weapons were handed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please explain to me: On page 5 of your statement, paragraph 1, you say that while you were in the administrative building of the Novi Izvor mine, some younger soldiers came, as you say, and asked that 10 by 10, as you said in the examination-in-chief go with them to search houses to see whether there were any weapons there and to check out all the houses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But from what you said, your number of 174 went down to 164, 162. Was that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The first time 11 men left and then another man was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to those 11?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They never came back. What happened to them, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 162 of you arrived in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know the exact number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know the exact number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Because there were 174 of us, 11 left, one was also taken out, so that's the number that remains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a name nicknamed Pufta among those who mistreated you over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention anyone else when you were talking to the investigators as having mistreated you apart from these Repic brothers, Zuca, and I don't know all their names. Do you remember anyone else? Can you give us any other names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Zoka, or Zokica, and someone who introduced himself as Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 8, paragraph 8, you say that this Zoka and Major shot Izet Hodzic in the knee and then ordered him to get lost and that he left and never returned. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who shot him in the knee; Zoka or the Major?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think it was the Major.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, how did Izet Hodzic leave if he was wounded in the knee? How could he walk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know myself, but he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wounded in the knee? Was his knee hit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 8, in paragraph 1, you say that four Muslims who said to this alleged Major -- was that a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's how they called him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they handed money to this Major and that they were released, that three of them went to Serbia and one stayed in Zvornik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why these three went to Serbia and one went to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who let them into Serbia? Were those the same men who had committed all those crimes that you enumerated in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know who let them leave your prison.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No. I wasn't with those men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Then I don't understand. How can you explain an event that you don't know how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I met those people when I left, when I was released after the prison. And then they told me that they had been transferred to Serbia and from there they went on somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that you met those people after you left Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, about these men who mistreated you and mutilated you and did all those horrors you described. Were they wearing any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Some were; some were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those who were, how many of them were wearing uniforms and how many were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think Zoka had a T-shirt with short sleeves, the Major sometimes, and they had camouflage trousers. As for the others, they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The others were in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Military uniform, whereas Repic had a special kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know how to explain it. It's a special kind of uniform. It's not camouflage like the army, it's a different kind of material. I don't know how to put it. It was a little thicker, like a woolen material.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand it that you heard from someone that this group was from Loznica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Zoka's group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: From people who were incarcerated in the Ciglana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: People who were held in the Ciglana of Novi Izvor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were they wearing any kind of insignia on those uniforms or the civilian clothes they wore or parts of clothing that they had on them? Did they have any markings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No. With the exception of Repic who had an insignia on his cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The traditional Serbian insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: In our language it's a cockade. What the real name of it is I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he wore a cockade on his cap. Was it clear to you then that this was a paramilitary formation of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I didn't know those men, and I didn't know who they were or what formation they belonged to. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they came to Celopek, you had occasion to see what they came in. Did they use a vehicle of some sort probably?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: We were shut up and we couldn't see whether they came in a vehicle or on foot. They entered on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me how many people this group consisted of, this Repic's group and this Major's group. How many men did it have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but roughly five or six of them would come at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five or six of them. I see. Please tell me, did you ever, while in Celopek, see a single person that you could assume belonged to the army of Yugoslavia or any kind of state body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just a few more questions about your stay in Batkovic. According to the information I have here, that camp in Batkovic was a kind of collection centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: There were about 1.500 men there from the surroundings of Zvornik, Kalesija, Vlasenica and Bratunac and the surrounding localities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of that camp? Who held it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which formation? Was it some army or some sort of police force? Who were the people in charge of Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The guards were military men, younger men. Later on, some older men came, again in military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, please, how many times did you see representatives of the Red Cross coming to visit the camp or collection centre or whatever we like to call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The first time they came -- after the first time, I think they came every 15 days, sometimes once a month, sometimes once a week. Up until the end they came to visit regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spent a whole year there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if they came sometimes once a week, sometimes once a month, sometimes once a fortnight, there must have been at least 20 visits over the period of one year, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, roughly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to talk to representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who spoke to them? Didn't they speak to the people who were captives there, who were detained there, imprisoned there, whatever you like to call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They did speak to some. They didn't speak to me personally, but they would more often than not bring us gifts. For example, personal hygiene kits, some clothing, cigarettes, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were exchanges carried out of prisoners from that collection centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes. I was in one of those exchanges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain and describe how you were exchanged. What was the actual procedure of your exchange?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think it was through the mediation of the Red Cross, actually. I was exchanged in Sibosnica, not far from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Through the Red Cross you were exchanged, you say. As far as I understand from the information I've been given, everybody was exchanged through the Red Cross. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to sign anything, make a statement of any kind, give some information to a Red Cross representative, your particulars, that kind of thing, and then he intervened with your exchange? What did this actual act of the exchange process look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, prior to the exchange, lists of persons were read out who were going up for the exchange. After that, we would be loaded up into buses and taken to the actual location where the exchange took place. We then crossed over into Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who drew up the lists of persons to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know, but the lists were read out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were in the group when you were exchanged? You weren't exchanged alone, I assume. There were a number of you, I assume, in one group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, approximately 300 to 400 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 300 to 400. Right. Now, in that one year that you spent in Batkovic, how many such groups were exchanged numbering so many people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I think that my group was the largest group that was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how many groups in all? On how many occasions did the exchange take place? Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know about one or two because I was in Batkovic. As to the others, I don't know, I wasn't there to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked at the beginning of your testimony about geography. That is to say you were asked to situate Zvornik, where Zvornik is and Mali Zvornik, one on one bank of the Drina, and the other on the other; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbs and Muslims lived in Zvornik; did they not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Mali Zvornik, the inhabitants were also mixed, Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zvornik is in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mali Zvornik is in Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was in Zvornik that the conflicts took place. That's right isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any conflict in Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of any mistreatment of Muslims by Serbs in Mali Zvornik across the bridge dividing Bosnia from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just take a look at my notes, if I may take a moment. Could you explain this to me, please, I didn't understand you very well: You described a rally, a meeting that took place in your village, and you say that the people or, rather, the local inhabitants rallied in front of the mosque. You remember that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I made a note of that here and said that about 100 people had rallied together. I think that's what you said. So how come of the 2.500 inhabitants, only about 100 rallied there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, I don't think everybody came to the rally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not everyone, only 100.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: There were just a hundred of them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what were the contents? What were the -- what was the rally held in aid of? What was the rally's slogan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The officer who was there asked that the weapons be handed over. If they didn't dare surrender their weapons officially, openly, then he pinpointed the stadium and told them that they could just leave their weapons there and leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the upshot of that request? Did they indeed leave their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, some weapons were handed over. I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I forgot to ask you something with respect to Batkovic. Do you happen to know whether anyone mistreated the detainees in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mistreated? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, they were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody mistreat you in Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What form did this mistreatment take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Blows, slaps. And when they would count us, I'd get a baton, a blow across my back, or when I was doing something, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know who held the centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have ten minutes left, if you need it, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I'll even need that long. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, Witness, in speaking about the fact that there were armed people in the village, that the police force was there. You mentioned the police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Which armed people are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I've made a note of this. After you spoke about the rally in front of the mosque and the demand that weapons be handed over, you said that there was some sort of police there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: The police came after the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Groome asked you what kind of police it was, a local police force or what, and your answer was yes, that it was the local police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They were wearing blue uniforms. I think it was the local police, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they people who had come from Zvornik or was there a police station in your village perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: We didn't have a police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many of those policemen turned up in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I would say roughly -- well, I don't know how many, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this then, please: You said that in the Drina Hotel a person wearing civilian clothes was issuing certificates of some kind or permits which would allow people free passage, and you said that they could even go to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that you yourself were given a certificate of that kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to have it with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't keep it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what it said on the certificate or permit? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, it was an ordinary piece of paper, small piece of paper on which -- I don't know the actual wording, but it said that the person holding the piece of paper could move around the town of Zvornik during a certain period of time, and the times were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a title? Did it mention the name of the authorities issuing the permit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it say the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik or the police station of Zvornik, or something like that, the Territorial Defence headquarters of Zvornik or anything else? Do you happen to remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any title at all? Was there a signature on the permit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, I don't think there was a signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all it contained was your name and surname and it said permit or certificate allowing you to move around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: It didn't say name and surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: It just said what it said, the words on the piece of paper. It said: "This is to allow movement around the country with ID papers."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a sort of temporary permit or certificate which served in place, in lieu of your ID papers, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: It was valid together with my ID card.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your ID card.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it had your name, surname, and your ID card number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No. All it said were the contents. Let me repeat again: "This is to certify that there is free movement around town with ID papers, valid ID papers." That's all, impersonal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me this: You told us here that the police was replaced by some sort of army. What soldiers? What army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They were people wearing military uniforms. Where they'd come from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any insignia or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Most probably they did, but I can't say now what they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained to us that you were taken in 11 busloads to Olovo and stopped in Han Pijesak because you weren't able to proceed because of the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then they took you back to Zvornik, and you went out to Tuzla and were stopped again because there was combat going on there too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they took you back to Zvornik once again, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the bus stop.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the authorities wanted to send you to some safe and secure territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's what they told us when they wanted to deport us. They said they would be transferring us and transporting us to Olovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did set out in the buses, and you were returned because you weren't able to reach Olovo physically or to reach Tuzla physically.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's what they told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would they have any reason to bus you around, drive you here and there, unless they were trying to actually transfer you to some other territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I can't really say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Branko Grujic, the mayor of Zvornik, addressed you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, he did address us in the Novi Izvor building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your second return; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, when we were separated from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you on that occasion? What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: He said we should write down the names of the people there, that we would go off on some work assignment and that we would sign a loyalty oath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nobody signed a loyalty oath of that kind, nor were you given these papers to sign; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not quite clear about this. How did you, from the authorities in Zvornik where you were under their control and you had contacts with the mayor of Zvornik, suddenly turned up in the hands of this criminal group, group of criminals that perpetrated all the acts that you described to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: That's not clear to me either. I don't know how we ended up there either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who took you to Celopek? Who took you over and transported you to Celopek? Did they come to Celopek once you were already there or did they come and take you off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: We were escorted by the army and police to Celopek, and these people would come to Celopek once we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the people that perpetrated the crimes you told us about appeared in Celopek once you were already there and incarcerated. That means they weren't in Zvornik, and they didn't take you to Celopek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, they didn't. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to the army and the police that took you to Celopek? Did they go back to Zvornik? They returned to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know where they went to after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who handed you over to these people? Was somebody there who handed you over to those people who perpetrated all those offences later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: We were incarcerated there, and in front of the entrance as far as we could see were armed policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those policemen, that police, were they present when they perpetrated the crimes you described to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: They were outside the compound and sometimes would enter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody try to prevent any one of these people who were later on arrested and taken to trial in Serbia, did anybody prevent them from committing the crimes they committed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Not in the hall. Outside, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any -- were any of the policemen in the hall? I assume that that belongs to the Zvornik municipality, Celopek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, Celopek is in Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, was anybody there from the police station in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how many real policemen were there except for that group of several people that you mentioned as being criminals? How many real policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: You mean real guards?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean the policemen you mentioned. I don't know who your guards were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Well, the police stood guard in front of the Dom, the centre. There might have been four or five of them, six perhaps. I don't know the exact number, but they were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must bring this examination to a close, but you can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, just try and focus on this and try and give me an explanation. What did that police have to do, those three or four policemen who stood guard there in Celopek? What did they have to do with the group who came to abuse you and mistreated you there? What were their links?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't know what they had to do with each other or whether they did have any connection at all. I know nothing about any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were they present when these people abused you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, not when these people were taken out. They were outside, however, when they were being beaten, when blows were struck. They would come in sometimes into the hall, in the premises where we were shut up in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did any of them try to protect you from the abuse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Perhaps one or two men, they did protect. One or two, these policemen who stood guard outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one or two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, just one or two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just two questions, Your Honour. But as a preliminary matter, I have searched the records using the transcript and I'm not able to locate that exhibit. If the accused would provide us with a copy of that or allow us to copy the document and inform us whether it's a document he received from us or from some other source, we will attempt to do a more thorough search of the exhibits this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, would you let us have that document and we'll exhibit it. Should in fact we find that it has been exhibited already, it can be deleted, but the safest course is to exhibit it now. If you would give us those orders, if you would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask, was this a document we provided the accused or was this a document he got on his own accord?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have the document, and I have already handed it over as an exhibit here. I can find a copy of it. I haven't got the copy with me now. I have these two copies of the orders on the part of the General Staff and 1st Army which I quoted from and which I also wanted to tender into evidence, but I think that Mr. Kwon did actually quote the exhibit that I've already handed over. Of course we can make a search to find copies and other documents referring to the same case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have -- we have covered the records of the court, Sabac court. We have not covered, as far as I can see, the orders which you referred to. Now, do you want those exhibited or not, the orders?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Hand them in, if you would, and we'll exhibit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence Exhibit dated the 1st of August, 1992 is Defence Exhibit 129. And then the order dated the 2nd of August, 1992 is Defence Exhibit 130. Re-examined by Mr. Groome:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in Batkovic camp, was your name recorded by the people who were detaining you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: You mean by the Red Cross. Yes, my name was recorded. They made a note of my name and surname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without saying your name, did you give them your true family name and first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it would appear from Defence Exhibit 150 -- sorry, Defence Exhibit 56, the comments made by the accused, and your testimony that you were in Batkovic for a year, it would appear that during the time this case was being investigated, you were in Batkovic, and my question to you is: During your time there, did anyone ever come and seek to interview you about what happened at Celopek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: No, nobody came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people who were detained in Celopek that subsequently were with you in Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were any of them interviewed about the crimes committed in Celopek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1461
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1461, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. And we will -- before you do, we will have to bring the blinds down. Is there some matter, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is a witness for whom the provisions -- the application for provisions of 92 bis have been applied. It will possibly be helpful to dispose of that application today so that we can plan the better for the use of tomorrow's time. The witness concerned has the benefit of some protection. He has a story, an account to give that is extremely powerful in many ways and one that any advocate would want to give in full, but the requirements that we deal with matters expeditiously make it a suitable witness to give via 92 bis for the majority of his evidence. There will only be a few matters that it might be helpful to take live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The problem is we -- we have this moment --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have only just this moment received the statement. It's very difficult to deal with it without having read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think there are two statements, an earlier one and later one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't on this occasion got back to the earlier practice of paragraph numbering the paragraphs in the statements. May I make this observation to assist in your consideration: In the application, a very large number of the paragraphs in each statement are identified as paragraphs that we would seek to lead in the ordinary viva voce way. It would only be in respect of very limited parts of those general paragraphs that I would wish to give viva voce evidence. Despite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the power of the statements made by this witness, I make the judgement that it is appropriate to take his evidence briefly if the Chamber is satisfied that 92 bis is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will look at that. Yes, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the next witness, is it? Just like the previous witness, I have understood that the opposite side wanted it to come under Rule 92 bis and that that application would be made today. I don't understand that practice, just as I don't understand the practice that a witness who was -- whose name and surname was listed is suddenly proclaimed to be a protected witness. This is, as the French would say -- it seems to be a la mode at the moment, that everybody wants to be a protected witness so that nobody can see their faces and that they could come and testify under special conditions. So I am categorically opposed to the fact that the next witness come under Rule 92 bis, because the application was made today whereas the witness is due to testify already tomorrow, which is quite unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider your objection and the circumstances. Mr. Kay, is there anything, briefly, you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court wanted to hear from me now or wait until you've looked at the papers. I can give a very short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In a sentence, what would be your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It isn't acts and conduct of the accused. It is cumulative. Prosecution concede that there should be cross-examination. It's the public interest element that the accused makes to the Court concerning the hearing of witnesses orally. I don't need to expand any further on those issues, having put it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will consider that and give our ruling in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the transcript should say it is not the acts and conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We will adjourn. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
